title: Lazy Demand And Stream Boundaries Checkpoint

questions.prompt: From [2,3,4,5,7], take the first two odd squares. How much input must the lazy fixture pull?

options.label: Pull only through the second qualifying value; eager mapping reads the full finite input.
Pull exactly two inputs because the result has length two.
Pull nothing because laziness makes all transformations constant-time.

questions.explanation: The lazy fixture reads 2,3,4,5 to produce 9 and 25, then stops before 7. Rejected inputs still need inspection. Eager filter/map evaluates the finite collection, and laziness does not eliminate transformation or predicate costs.

questions.prompt: A for...of loop breaks while consuming an opened generator with finally. What is the cleanup boundary?

options.label: Breaking for...of calls an available iterator return; a generator finally can release its owned resource.
Every iterable necessarily reopens after break with its resource still available.
Breaking disposes every unopened resource that might have been yielded later.

questions.explanation: Early exit calls an available iterator return, and the generator can execute finally for its owned state. A closed generator does not restart. This is not a promise that every iterator has cleanup or that unvisited resources are disposed.

questions.prompt: Node write returns false after a chunk is admitted. What follows?

options.label: Pause after write returns false; highWaterMark is a pressure threshold, not a strict total-memory cap.
Keep writing because false rejects the chunk without buffering it.
Assume the remote application has durably stored the chunk and memory cannot grow.

questions.explanation: False requests that the producer wait for drain; the chunk was admitted. Further writes can add buffered data, and highWaterMark is a threshold. Local buffering or drain does not establish the remote application durable effect.

questions.prompt: A four-byte upload chunk was accepted but its reply was lost. What should guide the next request?

options.label: Verify session and file identity, obtain the accepted offset, then send fresh bytes from that offset.
Replay the consumed body from zero until a success response appears.
Trust only the last client acknowledgement even if the server reports a later offset.

questions.explanation: The accepted offset can advance despite a lost reply. Bind it to the same session and file, then construct fresh bytes from that position. Reusing a consumed body or silently applying offset zero again can conflict or duplicate data.

questions.prompt: Does one Node top-level scheduling trace establish a universal timer/promise ordering?

options.label: Record the host and scheduling context; Node timer phases do not define every browser or module ordering.
Yes, one trace defines every browser, worker and module evaluation order.
Yes, a timer threshold guarantees an exact wall-clock execution deadline.

questions.explanation: Node phases, next-tick work, promise jobs and module context need explicit scope. A browser uses its own host rules. Timer thresholds permit later execution when callbacks occupy the thread; a single trace proves neither portability nor an exact deadline.
